subtopic: Miêu tả người / nơi / vật
question_text: You decided that you work. I would like to know about your company. What kind of company is it? When was it founded? Where is it located? What products or services does it offer?
expected_evidence: Trả lời thẳng đối tượng được hỏi ngay câu đầu
2–3 chi tiết cụ thể (vị trí, hình dáng, đặc điểm, con người)
Cảm nhận hoặc lý do cá nhân
Các câu nối với nhau thành đoạn (and, but, so, because, which)
answer_framework: Direct answer → overall picture → 2–3 details → what I like / feel
sample_answer_ih: Sure. I work for a large electronics company that makes smartphones and tablets. It's a foreign-invested company, and it's one of the biggest manufacturers in Vietnam. The factory I work at was built about ten years ago in an industrial park in Thai Nguyen province, which is around an hour from Hanoi. When it first opened, people in my hometown were really excited, because it created thousands of jobs for local people. These days, the factory produces millions of devices every year, and most of them are exported to countries all over the world, like the US, Europe, and other parts of Asia. Besides manufacturing, the company also has research and support teams, so there are many different kinds of jobs there. I'm in the quality team, and honestly, I'm proud to work for a company whose products people use every day.
sample_persona_vi: Nhân vật mẫu: khoảng 30 tuổi, làm kiểm tra chất lượng ở một nhà máy điện tử, sống ở căn hộ cùng vợ và con gái 5 tuổi. Hãy thay bằng chi tiết thật của bạn.

subtopic: Thói quen, hoạt động thường làm
question_text: Tell me about your daily routine at work. What kind of work do you engage in on a normal workday? What do you typically do as soon as you arrive at your office? Tell me everything about your day at work.
expected_evidence: Hiện tại đơn + trạng từ tần suất (usually, every…)
Trình tự rõ ràng (first, then, after that)
Chi tiết: khi nào, ở đâu, với ai
Lý do hoặc cảm nhận
answer_framework: How often → step by step → small details → why / how it feels
sample_answer_ih: Well, my workday usually starts at around a quarter to eight. As soon as I arrive, I change into my uniform, go through the security check, and then I check my email and the production plan for the day. At eight, my team has a short meeting where our leader tells us which models we're checking and whether there were any issues from the night shift. After that, I spend most of the morning on the line, inspecting product samples and recording the results in our system. Lunch is at noon in the company canteen, and that's usually the most relaxing part of the day, because I can chat with friends from other departments. In the afternoon, I do more inspections and sometimes help train new staff. Before I leave, I update my report so the next shift knows what's going on. Most days I finish at five, but when we have urgent orders, I stay a bit later.

question_text: Now, tell me about a project you did at work last week. What kind of project was it? How did it go? What did you have to do for the project? Did you have any meetings to attend for the project?

Chi tiết cụ thể và cảm xúc

answer_framework: When / where / who → what happened in order → feelings → result
sample_answer_ih: Last week, I was involved in a small but important project. Our team had to prepare for a customer audit, which means a group of people from a big customer came to check our quality process. It was pretty stressful at first, because we only had about five days to get ready. My job was to review our inspection records and make sure everything was complete and easy to follow. I also helped update a few work instructions that were a little out of date. We had three meetings during the week. In the first one, our manager explained what the customer wanted to see, and in the other two, we checked our progress and practiced answering questions. On the day of the audit, I was nervous, but everything went smoothly, and the customer was satisfied. So in the end, all the late nights were worth it.

There was a mango tree in the middle, and my friends and I used to play football there every afternoon until it got dark. My current home is really different. First of all, I live in an apartment in the city now, so it's much more modern and convenient. We have air conditioning, a washing machine, and a supermarket nearby, which we didn't have back then. On the other hand, my apartment is smaller, and there's no yard, so my daughter has to go to the park to play. I'd say my old house had more space and freedom, but my apartment is more comfortable.

sample_answer_ih: Last year, we decided to repaint my daughter's bedroom. On a Saturday morning, we moved all the furniture to the middle of the room and covered it with plastic sheets. I spent most of the day painting two layers, while my wife took our daughter out so she wouldn't get paint everywhere. It was tiring, but when she came back and saw her pink room, she was so excited. Lý do hoặc cảm nhận

sample_answer_ih: Besides talking to people, I use my phone for lots of things every day. In the morning, I check the weather and read news headlines. During the day, I use messaging apps a lot, because my team at work shares updates in a group chat. I also use my phone for payments. Almost every shop accepts QR codes now, so I rarely carry cash anymore. In the evening, I usually watch short videos or cooking videos on YouTube to relax. As for social media, I'm not very active. I only post photos on Facebook a few times a month, usually from family trips or special occasions. I don't play many games, but sometimes I play a simple puzzle game when I'm waiting for something. On weekends, I also use apps to order food, book taxis, and make video calls with my parents.

sample_answer_ih: These days, I don't make as many phone calls as I used to, because most of my friends prefer texting. But I still call my close friends maybe once or twice a week. When we talk, we usually start by asking about each other's families and work. Since most of us have small kids now, we often talk about our children, like their schools or funny things they did. We also talk about our plans, for example, when we can meet up for coffee or a weekend trip. Sometimes, if there's an important football match, we call each other to talk about it before and after the game. With my best friend, the calls are usually longer, because we talk about more serious things, like money, career plans, or problems at work. Talking on the phone helps us stay close, even though we're all busy.

There were a few things that made me choose it. First, the camera was really important to me, because I take a lot of photos of my daughter, and this phone has one of the best cameras in its price range. Second, the battery life was great, so I don't need to charge it during the day. Third, the price was reasonable, and there was a discount at the store when I bought it. Finally, I'd used the same brand before, so I was used to the system and it was easy to switch.

Students use them for studying, and office workers use them every day for their jobs. In many homes, there are also smart TVs, which people use to watch movies and YouTube. In recent years, some other kinds of technology have become more popular, like smartwatches, wireless earphones, and robot vacuum cleaners. Another big change is digital payment. People now pay with QR codes or banking apps almost everywhere, even at small street food stalls. So I'd say technology has really become a part of daily life in my country.

sample_answer_ih: One of my early memories about technology is my family's first mobile phone. It was a small Nokia phone that my father bought when I was about ten years old. I remember the only game on it was Snake, and my sister and I fought over who could play it. My father was very proud of that phone, and he kept it in a leather case. Compared to that, today's phones are completely different. They have huge touch screens, great cameras, and internet access, and you can do almost anything with them, like banking, shopping, and watching movies. The old phone was very simple, but its battery lasted almost a week, which is something I really miss about it.

question_text: Problems often come up because of our dependence on technology. Think about a time when you experienced a problem because some piece of technology was not working properly. Maybe your computer crashed or maybe your cell phone had no service. Tell me about a time when you had some kind of problem getting technology to work.

Sự cố cụ thể (chuyện gì đã sai)
Ít nhất 1–2 bước bạn làm để xử lý

answer_framework: Background → the problem → what I tried → result / lesson
sample_answer_ih: I had a problem with technology about six months ago, and it was really stressful. I was preparing an important presentation for a meeting with my manager. I worked on it for two days on my laptop. The night before the meeting, my laptop suddenly froze and then shut down completely. When I restarted it, I realized I hadn't saved the file for over an hour, and part of my work was gone. I panicked, because it was already eleven o'clock at night. First, I tried to find an automatic backup, but I could only recover an older version. So I had to stay up until almost two in the morning to redo the missing slides. Luckily, the presentation went well the next day. Since then, I always save my work to a cloud drive, and I've turned on automatic saving.

People sold everything there, like fresh vegetables, live chickens, fish in big buckets, clothes, and plastic toys. I remember the smell of fresh herbs mixed with the smell of fish. My mother always bargained with the sellers, which I found really interesting. My favorite part was the snack section, because if I behaved well, she would buy me a small cake or sweet soup. My impression was that it was a lively and exciting place, full of colors and sounds.

I was really confused at first, and then we both started laughing. The next morning, I went back to the store with the receipt and the box. The staff were very surprised and apologized many times. The staff usually ask for my ID card and give me some forms to fill out and sign. Sometimes they need to take a photo or my fingerprint for verification. After that, they process my request, which takes about ten to fifteen minutes. Finally, I check everything, thank the staff, and leave.

There were long wooden counters, and the staff sat behind glass windows. Everything was done on paper, and people had to wait in long lines, sometimes for an hour. I remember the staff counting stacks of cash by hand, which looked amazing to me. Banks today are completely different. They're bright, modern, and air-conditioned, and everything is done on computers. You take a number instead of standing in line. But the biggest difference is that now you can do most things on your phone, so you hardly need to go to the bank.

sample_answer_ih: Yes, I've been to Korea once, about two years ago, with my wife. The geography there was quite different from Vietnam. First of all, there are mountains almost everywhere, even inside cities. In Seoul, you can see mountains from many places, and people can go hiking right after work. In Vietnam, our mountains are mainly in the north, far from big cities like Hanoi. Second, Korea has four very clear seasons. I went in autumn, and the trees on the mountains were red and yellow, which was beautiful. In Vietnam, especially in the south, the weather is warm all year, and the leaves don't really change color. Third, Korea is a peninsula, so it has sea on three sides, while Vietnam has a long coastline on just one side. Both countries have beautiful nature, but in different ways.

Korean dramas, K-pop, and Korean food are extremely popular among young Vietnamese people, and many people are learning Korean to find better jobs. In sports, the relationship became famous when a Korean coach led the Vietnamese football team to some great achievements, which made many Vietnamese people love him. Now, there are also many marriages and friendships between people from the two countries.

Since then, Vietnam and Laos have often called their relationship a special friendship. Because of this, many Lao students come to study at Vietnamese universities, and Vietnam has helped build roads, schools, and hospitals in Laos. There's also a lot of trade between the two countries. I learned about this event in my history class in high school, and I think it's a good example of friendly cooperation between neighbors.

sample_answer_ih: In my country, recycling is becoming more common, but it's still developing. In big cities, people are encouraged to sort their household waste into different types, like recyclable waste, food waste, and other waste. Some apartment buildings, including mine, have separate bins for plastic, paper, and general trash. But the most common way of recycling in Vietnam is through scrap collectors. They go around neighborhoods on bicycles or motorbikes and buy things like old newspapers, cardboard boxes, plastic bottles, and metal cans. People usually save these things at home and sell them for a small amount of money. The collectors then sell them to recycling centers, where they're cleaned, melted down, and made into new products. Some schools and companies also organize recycling campaigns, where people bring old items in exchange for small gifts, like plants or notebooks.

When the bags are full, we sell them to a scrap collector who comes to our neighborhood every week, or we put them in the recycling bin in our building. Besides that, we reuse some things. For example, we use glass jars to store spices and dry food, and we use old T-shirts as cleaning cloths. We also try to reduce plastic bags by bringing our own reusable bags when we go to the supermarket. It's a small effort, but I think it helps.

On Sunday morning, I went down with a huge pile of boxes, and I saw that the paper container was completely full and boxes were all over the floor. Worse, the collection truck didn't come that Monday as planned because of a holiday. By Tuesday, the area was a big mess, and it even smelled bad because some people threw food waste in the wrong containers. Some residents complained in the building's group chat. My mother sold everything to her for a little money, and sometimes she let me keep the money to buy candy, which I loved. People also reused a lot of things back then, because they didn't have much money. For example, we used old cans as pencil holders, and my grandmother made bags from old rice sacks. So even though we didn't call it recycling, people were actually very good at not wasting things.

sample_answer_ih: The way recycling materials are collected has changed a lot over the years. In the past, there was no official recycling system in my country. They then sold these items to small recycling workshops, which often weren't very clean or safe. These days, things are becoming more organized. In big cities, there are now rules that require households to sort their waste into different categories, and many apartment buildings have separate bins for recyclables. Some companies have also started recycling programs, and there are more modern recycling factories. In addition, there are apps where you can book someone to pick up your recyclables. However, scrap collectors still play a big role, and many people still sell their recyclables to them. I think the system is improving, but slowly.

Many apps collect personal information, like phone numbers and locations, and sometimes this information is leaked, which leads to lots of spam calls. People are also worried about children, because kids can easily see harmful content or spend too much time online. These concerns have changed people's lives in some ways. People in their thirties and forties, like me, use the internet more for practical purposes, like work, online banking, and reading the news, although we also watch videos to relax. Older people, like my parents, use the internet more simply. They mainly use it to read the news, watch videos on YouTube, and make video calls with their children and grandchildren. I also had to sign a form. The officer gave me a receipt with the date when the card would be ready. About three weeks later, I received a message, and I went back to the office to pick up my new card.
